reports.content: We’re honored that Microsoft has once again been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM). As security environments grow more complex and attackers move faster, organizations need more than the ability to collect and analyze data. They need comprehensive visibility, context to understand what is happening, and the ability to act before an attack causes further damage. With more than 500 connectors across Microsoft and third-party solutions, Microsoft Sentinel brings together signals from across complex, multicloud environments. Its rich library of out-of-the-box detections, informed by Microsoft’s threat intelligence and organizational context, helps defenders identify sophisticated threats without building every detection from scratch. Microsoft Sentinel supports the core capabilities security teams depend on, from scalable security data management and advanced detection to threat hunting, investigation, and response. The Microsoft Sentinel data lake centralizes historical and real-time security data across platforms and clouds for cost-effective retention and advanced analytics at scale. Security operations center (SOC) optimization and cost management help teams improve coverage, identify detection gaps, and make informed decisions about the data they collect and retain. ISOC brings security operations and threat protection together, creating a unified foundation where people and AI agents can see, understand, and act across the environment. reports.title: Metasploit Wrap Up: Breaking Zimbra's Identity Boundaries
reports.summary: First up is a new shared mixin, Msf::Exploit::Remote::HTTP::Zimbra , which gives every current and future Zimbra module a common foundation for account/admin SOAP authentication, canonical identity resolution, mailbox-server lookup, and version parsing, allowing future modules to stay focused on the
reports.content: This release we have three pull requests from jburgess-r7 building out coverage for the identity-boundary issues detailed in Rapid7's Breaking Zimbra Identity Boundaries, Part One research. First up is a new shared mixin, Msf::Exploit::Remote::HTTP::Zimbra , which gives every current and future Zimbra module a common foundation for account/admin SOAP authentication, canonical identity resolution, mailbox-server lookup, and version parsing, allowing future modules to stay focused on the vulnerability instead of re-implementing Zimbra's SOAP plumbing. Built on top of that mixin are two new modules targeting CVEs from the same research track: CVE-2026-73571 ( #22080 ) It's an authorization bypass in Zimbra's SaveDraftRequest handling that lets an ordinary authenticated user send mail as another local mailbox without a delegation grant, landing a message in the victim's own Sent folder in the process. CVE-2026-93637 ( #22070 ) Is a rate-limit bypass in Zimbra's Network Edition GraphQL authentication endpoint, which lets credential-stuffing attempts skip the source-IP lockout counter that normally protects the SOAP login path. Both modules were validated against live Zimbra 10.1.16 Network Edition instances. Super cool contributions from our very own jburgess-r7 . The module supports optional Inbox delivery verification. reports.content: Overview On November 19, 2026, Broadcom published VMware Security Advisory VMSA-2026-0009 , addressing five vulnerabilities in VMware products. The most severe of these, CVE-2026-123890 , is an authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel ( CWE-288 ) in the VMware Directory Service component of vCenter. Broadcom assigned the vulnerability a critical CVSSv3 score of 9.8 . A malicious actor with network access to an affected vCenter deployment may exploit CVE-2026-123890 without credentials to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system as the Administrator user. Mandiant privately reported the issue to Broadcom. Also, Mandiant/Google Threat Intelligence confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by Chinese state-linked threat actor ARMORY CASTLE as early as September 2026. CVE-2026-123890 is distinct from the vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-59309 that Broadcom addressed earlier in 2026. The vendor FAQ states that all vCenter systems below the versions fixed by VMSA-2026-0009 require the new update, including systems that already received the earlier fix. Broadcom characterizes the vCenter update as an emergency change requiring prompt action. Mitigation guidance Vendor-provided updates are available for CVE-2026-123890. Broadcom lists no workaround, and the patches cannot be applied using vCenter Quick Patch. Organizations should prioritize upgrading vCenter on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles, using the standard update mechanism for their deployment. Without that follow-through, the immediate incident may be resolved while another attacker still has a way in. Preemptive managed detection and response (MDR) is Rapid7's approach to connecting exposure context, threat intelligence, AI-assisted investigation, and human expertise. It supports proactive cybersecurity by helping teams prioritize weaknesses before exploitation, investigate threats with a clearer understanding of risk, and use their findings to strengthen defenses. Many services also include proactive threat hunting and recommendations to improve security. Preemptive MDR connects that work more directly to what makes an organization vulnerable. In Rapid7’s model, exposure findings inform investigation and remediation priorities, while investigations reveal weaknesses that need attention. Security leaders gain a clearer connection between the threats their provider handles and the conditions their organization needs to address. reports.summary: Introduction For a threat actor, the perfect malware is one they don’t have to write, and already does all they need. reports.content: Introduction For a threat actor, the perfect malware is one they don’t have to write, and already does all they need. One example of this is shown by the China-aligned APT known as Webworm, which has been known to deploy the open-source SoftEther VPN into the networks of compromised governmental organizations to maintain low-profile, long-term access. After this was publicly documented and defenders could keep an eye out for this tactic, the actor presumably started thinking of ways to make their covert access stealthier. In this post, we share our analysis of what we believe to be a so-far unknown custom SoftEther-based tool, which implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools, and which we attribute to Webworm with moderate confidence. We additionally provide guidance and tooling for detecting its presence on a system and extracting the configuration(s) associated with it. Technical analysis To illustrate how the tool works, we will use the only public sample of this tool we are aware of, which can be found in our IoCs list ( 90e7… ). The sample is a Windows PE32+ file targeting the x64 architecture. Based on cleartext strings and constants in the binary, we identified it as a (modified) build of the SoftEther VPN Bridge executable, specifically version 4.44, build 9807. Similarly, the PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb . As such, the tool doesn’t hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions. The first and most trivial change the threat actor implements is in the PE metadata. Here we learn that the OriginalFileName of this binary is netcapa.exe , and it brands itself as “Network Monitor Software” published by a company named “Network Systems Solutions Inc.“. CVE ID Description CWE CVSSv4 CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 flow-control memory corruption permitting worker-context RCE CWE-191 (Integer Underflow) 9.2 (Critical) nginx can miscalculate how much response data an HTTP/2 client has allowed it to send. A remote, unauthenticated client can exploit this error by cancelling queued response data, then make nginx use an invalid length when copying a later response. The resulting memory corruption can disclose data, interrupt service, and execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions. Impact Rapid7 has developed a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated RCE against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8 , as shown below in Figure 1. The target nginx server’s configuration had http2 on and TLS enabled. Note that for brevity, video playback is at 8x speed. reports.title: The challenge of defending against bulletproof dead drops on public blockchains
reports.summary: The evolution of malware command-and-control (C2) infrastructure has shifted away from fragile, centralized servers and hardcoded domains toward resilient, decentralized blockchain networks that eliminate single points of failure. Threat actors are leveraging immutable public ledgers such as Bitcoin
reports.content: The evolution of malware command-and-control (C2) infrastructure has shifted away from fragile, centralized servers and hardcoded domains toward resilient, decentralized blockchain networks that eliminate single points of failure. Threat actors are leveraging immutable public ledgers such as Bitcoin transactions, EVM smart contracts via techniques like EtherHiding, TRON wallets, and Solana memo programs to store, mask, and persistently update their operational endpoints. By executing read-only remote procedure call (RPC) queries to retrieve encrypted C2 configurations directly into compromised endpoint memory, adversaries can continuously bypass traditional perimeter defenses and domain seizures. Modern cybersecurity requires a fundamental shift away from static domain blocklists toward monitoring anomalous outbound JSON-RPC traffic, analyzing endpoint memory, and treating blockchain infrastructure as an active threat communication channel. The command-and-control (C2) channel is the operational backbone of any persistent malware campaign. It is also the most fragile component. The moment an actor's C2 infrastructure is identified and reported to the hosting provider, the domain registrar, or law enforcement, the campaign's operational capability collapses. This fundamental asymmetry, where defenders need to identify only a single infrastructure link to disrupt an operation, has driven a multi-decade arms race in resilience techniques, spanning from fast flux DNS evasion to decentralized and peer-to-peer architectures. Traditional C2 infrastructure where malware beacons to a hardcoded domain or IP address is volatile by design. Security researchers or incident responders who identify the C2 address can trigger a response. The hosting provider can null-route the IP addresses and the domain registrars can suspend malicious domains under abuse policies, law enforcement can obtain court orders compelling infrastructure seizure, and threat intelligence vendors push blocklist updates that cut off the malware from its C2 links across several compromised endpoints simultaneously. This single point of failure model renders sophisticated malware families inactive once their C2 is identified and sinkholed. By redirecting malware traffic to researcher-controlled servers, researchers can not only disrupt the botnet but map the full victim community, gather forensic telemetry, and notify affected organizations. reports.content: Update 11/18/2026: Cisco has released a security advisory on products potentially affected by this vulnerability. Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK Java (CVE-2026-114938), dubbed “Java4Shell,” with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 that may lead to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). This vulnerability can be triggered by sending a malformed Base64 input to affected JVMs, which can result in RCE. Details This vulnerability affects OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed. This vulnerability does require a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI; these include commonly deployed processors from both Intel and AMD, resulting in a large potential attack surface of vulnerable systems, including both on-premise and cloud environments. Cisco Talos would like to thank Calif.io for sharing the details of the vulnerability in advance of public disclosure . Observed exploitation Talos has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure. Talos will continue to monitor for exploitation attempts and will provide updates accordingly. Recommendations and guidance Talos recommends applying the software update for this vulnerability. If immediate patching is not possible, other mitigations can be implemented in the interim. The primary mitigation is starting the JVM with AVX-512 support disabled. This can be done by starting the application with “=XX:UseAVX=2”. Note that this is only applicable for x86-64 systems, as ARM-based processors will not recognize the command, likely resulting in failure to start. The vulnerability, dubbed “ Java4Shell ” by finders Calif, can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash a Java application or execute code with the privileges of its Java process. Oracle rates the vulnerability High, with a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1 and high attack complexity, in its November security advisory . Affected OpenJDK runtimes enable the vulnerable Base64 optimization by default when the Java virtual machine (JVM) can use the required x86-64 CPU features, including AVX-512 VBMI. A Java application exposes the flaw when it passes untrusted data to that optimized decoder. For example, a web service may decode HTTP Basic credentials before it checks the username and password. Red Hat reports no known exposure on ARM64 or on x86-64 processors without AVX-512 VBMI in its OpenJDK bulletin . Calif’s disclosure states that they demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against several popular Java based applications, and they have published a local proof of concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-114938, which can test if a local JDK is vulnerable. Given the ubiquitous nature of Java and its deployment across enterprise environments, Rapid7 recommends identifying and remediating affected systems, with a focus on Internet exposed systems, on an emergency basis and outside of normal patching cycles. Rapid7 is actively monitoring the situation and will update this blog as new information arrives. For the latest vendor release information, refer to Oracle's November security update notice and OpenJDK's vulnerability advisories . When frequently used Base64 decoding code is compiled, HotSpot can substitute a native routine that processes multiple bytes at once. The vulnerable path requires an x86-64 runtime, CPU features including AVX-512 VBMI , and effective JVM settings that permit the optimizing compiler and Base64 intrinsic. Instead of stealing a password, an attacker persuades someone to approve a sign-in on a legitimate site simply by entering a code. The resulting access often can reach email, files, or other cloud services, depending on the account and the permissions granted. Notable earlier campaigns such as EvilTokens show how readily this technique can be scaled to do real damage. Microsoft worked hard with partners in industry and law enforcement to disrupt EvilTokens in September 2026. Access private repositories available to the affected account. reports.content: In this article Phishing attack overview Attack chain overview Mitigation and protection guidance References Learn More On November 13, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organizations across multiple sectors worldwide. The messages created a false sense of urgency by claiming that emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them. This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures. Microsoft Defender blocks malicious domains used in this campaign, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines phishing emails. Apache Axis is a Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) implementation used for the creation of Java Web services. CISA has assigned CVE-2026-90436 a CVSS score of 9.8 Critical . Since the initial November 6 disclosure, it has transpired that some versions of Atlassian Confluence Data Center and N-able N-central use the affected Axis library and are vulnerable to CVE-2026-90436. Separately, on November 13, 2026, N-able reported exploitation in the wild against N-central for a vulnerability that strongly correlates to CVE-2026-90436. reports.content: Overview As part of our research into Zimbra Collaboration Suite , Rapid7 reported five findings in ONLYOFFICE Docs. An attacker with view-only access to a document can chain vulnerabilities in ONLYOFFICE Docs to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root inside the official DocumentServer container. The findings also expose server files and document data that the viewer never displays, even when downloading is disabled. CVE Finding CVSS CVE-2026-113627 DocBuilder native file read and Session JWT forgery 7.1 High CVE-2026-110385 DocBuilder SaveFile conversion parameter injection and code execution 8.7 High CVE-2026-97727 Complete-save format path traversal and arbitrary file write 6.5 Medium CVE-2026-113630 Root-helper command injection 7.8 High CVE-2026-113631 View-only export of non-rendered document data 6.5 Medium ONLYOFFICE confirmed on October 23, 2026 that all five findings were fixed in Document Server 10.0. The changelog describes the release's security changes. Proof-of-concept code is available on the accompanying Github repository . Product description ONLYOFFICE Docs provides online viewers and editors for documents, spreadsheets, presentations, forms and PDFs. It supports collaborative editing and can integrate with applications that store and share files. An integrating application, for example Zimbra Collaboration Suite, supplies an opening configuration identifying the document and the user's permissions, signed with the Browser key. This client-visible credential is referred to below as the Editor JWT. After opening a document, DocumentServer issues a Session JWT for reconnecting and saving. Incoming service requests, including document-building jobs, are validated using ONLYOFFICE's Inbox JWT key. DocumentServer can also send generated document output to the integrating application's callback URL. reports.content: Cisco Talos is tracking the growing in-the-wild usage of AI-enabled penetration testing frameworks. reports.content: When comparing MDR pricing, it helps to understand what the same annual budget would buy from each provider. Two proposals with similar prices may give analysts access to different evidence, retain it for different periods, or leave your team with different responsibilities. Those differences can affect what happens when you need to investigate a compromised account or trace an attacker’s low-and-slow activity across your environment. For security leaders weighing asset-based against ingestion-based pricing, a useful comparison starts with the systems you need to protect and the logs required to investigate threats. Giving providers the same requirements and budget helps expose the decisions behind each quote, including what you would need to exclude or pay more to include. Asset-based vs. ingestion-based MDR pricing Under asset-based pricing, the charge is tied to a defined population of assets. You need to establish how the provider counts workstations, servers, cloud resources, and other systems, alongside which data sources and service capabilities the price includes. A predictable asset count can help with budgeting, but the proposal still needs to explain any integration limits or additional service charges. At Rapid7, an asset is defined as any physical or virtual endpoint or server running a supported operating system within the monitored environment. With ingestion-based pricing, some of the cost depends on the volume of data collected or processed. The comparison needs to account for the included allowance, how billable volume is measured, and what happens when usage increases. Retention, search, and supporting infrastructure may also contribute to the overall cost, depending on the commercial model. At Rapid7, MDR customers have access to 13 months hot storage of logs as standard. Whichever approach you are evaluating, include the technology, analysts, and response support needed to deliver the service. A SIEM ingestion charge on its own cannot be compared directly with an MDR subscription that includes investigation and response. Both proposals need to account for the work your organization expects the provider to perform - this clarity is key to a successful partnership. I don't know the answers, but a few days ago I didn't know there were questions.” – Terry Pratchett The one big thing Cisco Talos is breaking down a huge Microso
reports.content: Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter. Back in college, I took an anthropology course called “Peoples and Cultures of Southeast Asia.” While the title sounded like your everyday anthro course, this one was a little different. It had fewer students, maybe around 10, and took place from 7 – 9 p.m., most college kids’ nightmare — but it was the perfect time of day to videochat with Malaysian students on the other side of the globe with a 12-hour time difference. My university had a 14-week semester, while the university in Kuala Lumpur had seven weeks, so our class had time before meeting the students to study Malaysia’s pre- and post-colonial history, political climate, and cultural and religious dynamics; watch famous Petronas Deepavali and Chinese New Year ads ; and (of course) drool over pictures of nasi lemak and teh tarik. When both classes began videochatting with one another (yeah, we used Zoom before it was cool), our questions were quite tame. This was partly because we were afraid of offending one another, and partly due to some thorny laws around political speech. They’d ask, “Where do you store your winter clothes during the summer? They’re so puffy!” or “How often do you eat at McDonald’s?” We’d ask, “What's your favorite food at pasar malams (night markets)?” and “How do you deal with the heat and humidity?” (The answer to that one: Malaysia, which is around the size of New Mexico, has around 1,000 shopping malls with heavenly air conditioning.) Over the weeks, with encouragement from our professors, a few brave souls from both countries began to open up about their opinions on the government, social justice movements, discrimination, and more. Their vulnerability was contagious and soon encouraged others to speak up more in class, and everyone began to ask more pointed questions. They’d ask, “What is it like to be openly LGBT+ in the U.S.?” We’d ask, “Do you think the new political party gaining the prime ministership will bring more change?” We soon developed a class motto: Never be afraid to ask questions. I firmly believe that questions asked in good faith create a space where it is safe to be curious, when everyone understands that the goal is understanding, not judgment. It’s perfectly fine to be honest about your lack of knowledge, and you’re always allowed to decline a question if the topic is too complex or personal to unpack in the moment. reports.content: In this article Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse tools Model poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transfer What the studies show about agent backdoors Mitigation and protection guidance Securing agents beyond the model References Learn More As organizations increasingly deploy specialized AI agents, trust cannot depend solely on a model behaving as expected during evaluation or normal use. As Satya Nadella has argued in Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era , trustworthy enterprise AI requires independent observability and controls that sit outside the model. Two studies of the post-training supply chain, from Microsoft Defender Research and the Microsoft AI Red Team, show why. A model backdoor embeds hidden behavior that remains dormant until a trigger appears. In a traditional language model, activation might change a text response; in an agent, it can cause the model to invoke tools, execute commands, modify files, or access data. The two studies examine attacks with different levels of access. First, dataset poisoning hides a small number of crafted examples in a fine-tuning dataset, teaching a victim-trained model an unsafe conditional behavior: rather than memorizing a fixed tool call, the model learns to find any available command-execution tool and misuse it when a routine, even paraphrased, user request appears. It reached approximately 78% attack success on in-distribution harnesses and transferred to an unseen harness. Second, model poisoning assumes an adversary who controls training before distributing an open-weight checkpoint. This allows the adversary to optimize backdoor reliability while minimizing degradation in general performance by combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). In this setting, average success on unseen repositories reached 84.1% to 94.8%, with additional transfer across coding harnesses. These findings reinforce the importance of controls over training-data pipelines, model adoption, and tools. Introduction Coding and terminal agents do more than generate text. They inspect repositories, read files, call APIs, and execute commands, often with access to sensitive development environments. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts shou
reports.content: In this article When one RCE stops being just one RCE Observed attack chains How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address Mitigation and protection guidance References Learn More Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. When one RCE stops being just one RCE Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it. To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions. GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it. Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself. The codename MDASH scans produced 26,502 raw scan findings in about two wee
reports.content: In this article From scans to reports Selected findings Closing thoughts At Microsoft’s FORGE Lab , we used codename MDASH to scan a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026. One full-time researcher and one intern led this three-month effort, which has so far produced 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs . We confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline. Finding the bugs was only part of the work. The initial scans produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, but turning those results into reproducible bugs, upstream reports, and patches took months of expert investigation and collaboration with Linux maintainers. reports.content: Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than 10 neurons to inject a short payload. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker’s command. And because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party models and internally developed models. Key findings from Microsoft Research include: Software abuse and manipulation are familiar threats. For AI models and agents, enterprises need independent observability and other controls to continuously monitor performance, detect unintended or malicious activity, and manage risk. Satya Nadella recently outlined this approach in a blog post . A backdoored model can pass evaluations. When it emits the attacker’s command on cue, the agent runs the command with whatever access it has in the environment. The attack needs inference-only compute. If a machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it. Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously. Microsoft has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. However, this research aligns with similar recent research by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively, highlighting the need to audit open weights like code. Notably, Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. Using frontier agents as auditors can help automate the defense against this threat. More broadly, Microsoft Research’s approach demonstrates an adaptable process for securing AI agents: agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. reports.content: Microsoft is publishing 1,092 own-product vulnerabilities on November 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 745 vulnerabilities in Windows. Until a few months ago, these volumes would have been unimaginable, but if anything, this month feels like a slight reprieve. The jury is still out on whether patching many more vulnerabilities will lead to better security outcomes; every code change to resolve a known vulnerability could easily introduce new hidden treasure for researchers or threat actors to unearth in the future. Despite the vast uptick in volume during 2026, there has been no accompanying increase in the number of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, with no known public disclosure at all this month. Outlook: zero-day spoofing Imagine coming home and checking your mailbox to find a postcard. You admire the non-specific image of a tropical beach at sunset, and flip it over to scan the handwriting on the back, which looks vaguely familiar. It’s addressed to you, but you can’t make out the signature, and the message is short and generic. Is that real handwriting, or has this been printed? Probably marketing material. You put the card in the recycling and, since life is busy, you move on and forget about it. Somehow, you remain entirely unaware that, immediately after reading the postcard, you took out your phone and sent high-resolution images of your front door key to a number you’ve never contacted before. Is this sketch just some rather questionable science fiction? Yes, hopefully, but what if that non-specific postcard was instead a malicious file in your Outlook inbox? Now we’re talking about CVE-2026-124194 , an exploited-in-the-wild spoofing vulnerability. Merely opening a specially crafted malicious file causes Outlook to silently connect to an attacker-controlled location and leak the user’s NTLM v2 hash. All supported versions of classic Outlook receive patches. The relatively low CVSS v3.1 base score of 6.5 does not tell the full story here, since this vulnerability provides value for both commodity attackers working to harvest initial access at scale, and also more targeted campaigns by more sophisticated threat actors. reports.content: Overview On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central , its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform. In a public disclosure titled Able2Shell, an independent researcher has published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code covering 33 issues. According to the disclosure, the issues include unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE), privilege escalation to root, credential disclosure, and unauthorized account creation. One unauthenticated chain combines XML external entity (XXE) and session-handling weaknesses to execute code as the nable service account. Other demonstrated chains involve an administrator viewing malicious patch metadata or use ProductAdmin credentials. Rapid7 Intelligence is currently triaging the newly published details. Before the hotfix release on November 10, N-able reported scanning activity associated with the published PoC code and said it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited. The vendor advised keeping N-central deployments offline while it developed and validated a hotfix. Hosted N-central classic environments were offline, according to the same notice. That notice did not yet include CVE identifiers or CVSS scores. N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to administer endpoints and infrastructure. Compromise of an RMM server can put downstream managed environments at risk. N-central has previously been targeted through separate vulnerabilities, including an authentication bypass covered by Rapid7 in August 2026 . Given the platform's administrative reach and the availability of public exploit code, Rapid7 recommends treating the current disclosure as an emergency. Consider the last significant investigation: did it lead to a clearer detection, a stronger response plan, or a better underst
reports.content: Your managed detection and response (MDR) provider flags suspicious activity, and your analyst spends the next hour finding the account, checking logs, and deciding whether anything needs to happen. By the time the investigation is underway, the alert feels less like help and more like a task assignment. MDR should bring your team capacity and expertise when it needs them. If the service keeps handing the hardest work back to your analysts, these five signs can help you work out where the arrangement is falling short. 1. Every alert arrives with homework If your analysts are still sorting through the same recurring false positives, the extra coverage may be creating more work than it removes. Even an alert worth investigating is only so useful when your team has to gather the basic context before it can make a decision. Take a few recent alerts and look at what your provider had already checked when it contacted you. You should be able to see how it separated routine activity from a credible threat, and what it did to stop familiar noise from coming back. 2. It spots the fire, but cannot see the fuel A suspicious login involving an account with broad access deserves a different response from the same activity on a tightly restricted account. The systems within reach, their importance to the business, and any known weaknesses all help determine what needs attention first. When your MDR leaves your team to assemble that picture during an investigation, valuable time goes into finding context that could have informed the response from the start. Find out how your provider uses information about assets, identities, vulnerabilities, and current threats, including what it can help you address before an incident occurs. 3. Your team gets incident updates, but few useful lessons When a provider contains a threat and closes the case, your team should come away with more than a record of what happened.
